summary: The note surveys shape-shifting legends across cultures (werewolves, Japanese kitsune and tanuki, Navajo skinwalkers, and modern media shapeshifters) as mirrors of the human psyche. Each section pairs a myth with an expert's interpretation, covering emotional duality, rage and social taboo, trickery and wisdom, power and morality, and identity. It concludes that these myths endure because they reflect universal human experiences of duality and self-understanding.
one_line: Shape-shifting legends from werewolves to kitsune and skinwalkers are examined as reflections of human duality, morality, and identity, with expert commentary.
key_facts: On October 14, 2023, psychologist Dr. Eileen Richards gave a lecture titled 'Shape-Shifting Lore and the Human Mind: A Symbiotic Relationship', saying shapeshifters act as "mirrors to our emotional duality".

On November 29, 2023, at the International Symposium on Mythological Creatures, folklore specialist Dr. Marcus O'Reilly said the werewolf myth portrays tension between civilized selves and primal urges.
Werewolf legends tie the full moon, a traditional symbol of change and insanity, to the loss of human rationality.
Werewolf tales usually feature people cursed with lycanthropy who transform against their will, and the subsequent remorse echoes guilt after actions taken in anger.
Dr. Aiko Tanaka published findings on December 7, 2023, in the Journal of Mythological Studies, saying the kitsune (fox) and tanuki (raccoon dog) are respected rather than feared as monsters.
Kitsune and tanuki in Japanese folklore take human forms to trick, deceive, and occasionally impart wisdom, representing adaptability, intelligence, and the multifaceted nature of truth.
In Navajo lore, skinwalkers are sorcerers who transform into animals, are feared for their powers and moral corruption, and willingly don animal skins, often to harm others secretly.
Interviewed on January 21, 2024, Navajo elder and cultural historian Jonathan Yazzie said skinwalkers are warnings about spiritual knowledge and power applied selfishly.
In a February 15, 2024 interview, Dr. Laura Palmer, an expert in modern mythology, said contemporary shapeshifters embody the search for identity in an increasingly complex world.
Modern cinema, television, and literature use shape-shifting as a metaphor for identity, alienation, and transformation.
The note concludes that shapeshifter myths share deep psychological roots and act as mirrors of hidden desires, fears, and the dual natures all humans harbor.
